title: Skills & Innovation Academy Ghana 2026: GIZ Opens 5-Day Employability Training for Graduates in Greater Accra, Bono, Northern and Upper West
summary: Applications are now open for the Skills Innovation Academy 2026 , an intensive five-day professional development programme designed to help graduates strengthen their technical and soft skills and improve their readiness for the world of work. The current application round targets graduates based in four regions of Ghana: Greater Accra Bono Northern Region Upper West Region The Academy is an initiative of Invest for Jobs – Special Initiative “Decent Work for a Just Transition” , an initiative of Germany’s Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ) and implemented by the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH . GIZ Ghana’s current call describes the programme as an intensive five-day technical and soft-skills training aimed at improving participants’ employability. The application deadline is: 23 September 2026 Interested candidates can submit their applications through the official registration form. Apply for the Skills Innovation Academy 2026 About the Skills Innovation Academy The Skills Innovation Academy is a short, intensive employability training initiative designed to help graduates strengthen the practical skills needed to transition more effectively into employment. The current September 2026 call invites graduates from Greater Accra, Bono, Northern and Upper West who want to upgrade their skills and improve their employability. Participants will take part in five days of technical and soft-skills training focused on preparing them for the demands of the workplace. The programme is particularly relevant to graduates who may already have academic qualifications but want additional practical preparation before entering or progressing in the labour market. It reflects a wider challenge facing many young graduates: completing formal education does not always mean that a person has had sufficient opportunities to develop the practical, interpersonal and workplace skills employers expect. The Academy therefore seeks to help bridge the space between: Academic learning and employment Technical knowledge and workplace application Qualifications and job readiness Graduate potential and employer expectations Who Is Behind the Skills Innovation Academy? The Academy is linked to Invest for Jobs – Special Initiative “Decent Work for a Just Transition.” The initiative is supported by the Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development of Germany, BMZ , and implemented by GIZ . The current call was published by GIZ Ghana. GIZ is Germany’s international cooperation agency and works with governments, private-sector institutions, civil society and other partners on programmes connected to areas such as: Employment Economic development Skills Governance Sustainability Private-sector development Innovation Within Ghana, the Skills Innovation Academy fits particularly closely with employment and workforce-development objectives. What Is Invest for Jobs? Invest for Jobs is associated with the German development cooperation initiative focused on supporting decent employment and sustainable economic development . For graduates, programmes supported under this framework may be particularly valuable because they focus not only on education in the abstract, but on the transition into actual economic and professional opportunities. The Skills Innovation Academy therefore emphasizes practical preparation for work rather than purely academic instruction. What Does the Programme Offer? The current call describes the Academy as an: Intensive 5-day technical and soft-skills training programme. Its central objective is to equip participants with practical skills that can help them function more effectively in the workplace and compete for employment opportunities. The programme combines two broad areas: 1. Technical Skills Technical skills are the practical or job-related capabilities people need to perform professional tasks. The exact technical modules for the September 2026 cohort are not listed in the public announcement provided by GIZ Ghana. Applicants should therefore avoid assuming that a specific technology, profession or vocational field is guaranteed unless it is stated in the registration form or communicated directly by programme organizers. The important point from the current call is that technical training forms part of the five-day programme. 2. Soft Skills Soft skills refer to the interpersonal and professional behaviours that help employees function successfully in organizations. These can generally relate to areas such as: Communication Teamwork Professionalism Problem-solving Workplace behaviour Adaptability Collaboration Self-management However, the current public call does not publish a detailed list of the September cohort’s exact soft-skills modules. Applicants should therefore rely on the current registration materials for the definitive curriculum. Why Soft Skills Matter for Graduates Employers often evaluate candidates on more than academic qualifications. A graduate may have strong academic knowledge but still need to develop the ability to: Communicate clearly Collaborate with colleagues Manage responsibilities Present ideas professionally Adapt to workplace expectations Solve practical problems Demonstrate initiative This is one reason short employability programmes can be useful during the transition between education and work. The Skills Innovation Academy specifically positions itself around strengthening employability through both technical and interpersonal development. The Academy Is Focused on Practical Employability The wording of the current call is important. GIZ Ghana does not describe this as a theoretical academic course. It says the training is intended to equip participants with practical skills for the world of work . That means the Academy should be particularly relevant to individuals who want to become more workplace-ready. Potential participants may include graduates who are: Searching for their first job Preparing for employment Trying to strengthen their professional profile Looking to build practical skills after graduation Seeking to improve confidence in professional environments Preparing to transition into a new career area Programme Duration The Skills Innovation Academy lasts: Five days The training is described as intensive, meaning participants should expect a concentrated learning schedule rather than a long-term part-time programme. Applicants should ensure that they can commit to the programme once selected. The current public announcement does not specify the exact training dates or daily schedule, so selected participants should rely on instructions from GIZ or the implementing team. Is This a Job? No. The Skills Innovation Academy is a training and employability development programme . Applicants should not interpret participation as: A job offer Guaranteed employment An internship A paid position Its purpose is to strengthen participants’ skills and employability. The public call does not state that completion automatically results in placement with an employer. Is This a Scholarship? No. The opportunity is not advertised as an academic scholarship. Participants are not applying for: University tuition A degree Research funding Academic study abroad Instead, they are applying for a short professional skills-development programme. Is There a Stipend or Financial Allowance? The current September 2026 public call does not state that participants will receive a stipend, transport allowance, accommodation allowance or cash payment . It also does not publicly specify: Training fee Accommodation provision Meals Transport support Certificate Employment guarantee Applicants should therefore avoid assuming that these benefits are included unless the registration form or organizers confirm them. This is especially important when promoting the opportunity: it should not be described as “fully funded” based solely on the currently published announcement. Current Target Regions The September 2026 call specifically targets graduates in: Greater Accra Greater Accra is Ghana’s main administrative and economic centre and includes Accra and its surrounding metropolitan areas. Graduates living in this region form one of the target groups for the current round. Bono Region Graduates in the Bono Region are also invited to participate. Northern Region The current programme expands access to graduates in Northern Ghana through inclusion of the Northern Region. Upper West Region Graduates based in Upper West are also among the target participants. The geographical targeting is therefore not nationwide in the current announcement. A Region-Based Programme Model The Skills Innovation Academy appears to use different regional application rounds. For example, an earlier GIZ Ghana round in June 2026 targeted applicants in: Greater Accra Eastern Region Volta Region and described eligibility for that particular round as SHS graduate or higher . The current September round is different: it specifically names: Greater Accra Bono Northern Upper West and simply refers to applicants as graduates . Applicants should therefore follow the requirements of the current September 2026 call , rather than assuming that every criterion from an earlier regional round automatically applies. What Academic Qualification Is Required? The current public announcement asks: “Are you a graduate in the Greater Accra, Bono, Northern Upper West…” However, it does not publicly define the precise educational level meant by “graduate” in the current call. For example, the announcement does not explicitly state whether the September round requires: SHS completion Diploma HND Bachelor’s degree University degree Any post-secondary qualification An earlier 2026 round explicitly said SHS graduate or higher , but the current September announcement does not repeat that exact wording. Therefore, applicants should complete the official form and follow the current eligibility questions rather than assuming a specific tertiary degree is compulsory. Is There an Age Limit? The current Skills Innovation Academy announcement does not state an age limit . It does not publicly specify: Minimum age Maximum age A youth age bracket such as 18–35 Therefore, an age restriction should not be added to promotional material unless it appears in the current application form. Is Work Experience Required? The current call does not state a minimum work-experience requirement. Applicants are therefore not publicly required to have: One year of experience Two years of experience Prior professional employment Previous internship experience The programme is presented around strengthening graduate employability, which suggests that it is particularly relevant to people at an early stage of their careers. What Fields of Study Can Apply? The current announcement does not restrict participation to one academic field. It does not state that candidates must be graduates of: STEM Business Engineering IT Humanities Social sciences or another specific discipline. The wording is broad: graduates seeking to improve their skills and employability . Applicants from different academic backgrounds may therefore consider applying, unless the registration form contains additional track-specific requirements. What Participants Could Gain Although the current call does not publish an exhaustive list of outputs, the programme is designed to improve participants’ readiness for employment. Potential professional value includes: Stronger Workplace Skills Participants can develop a better understanding of the behaviours and practical abilities needed in professional environments. Improved Technical Capacity The programme includes technical-skills training alongside soft skills. Greater Employability The Academy is explicitly marketed as an opportunity to upgrade skills and improve employability. Professional Development A concentrated skills programme can help graduates identify areas requiring further development before applying for jobs. Why Employability Training Matters The transition from education into employment can be difficult, particularly where graduates have limited opportunities to gain workplace experience. Common challenges can include: Limited practical experience Lack of familiarity with workplace expectations Difficulty translating qualifications into job-ready skills Weak interview preparation Limited professional networks Insufficient soft-skills training Programmes such as the Skills Innovation Academy seek to strengthen the practical side of graduate preparation. How to Apply Applications are submitted through the official online registration form. Apply for the Skills Innovation Academy 2026 Candidates should provide accurate information and carefully review all questions before submitting. The public call also notes that applicants can register through the QR code displayed on the programme flyer. Application Deadline The deadline is: 23 September 2026 GIZ Ghana’s current public announcement confirms this closing date. Applicants should consider submitting early in case they experience: Connectivity problems Form errors Missing documents Last-minute technical difficulties How to Prepare Before Applying 1. Review Your Educational Information Have accurate details of your: Educational institution Qualification Field of study Graduation status ready before beginning. 2. Be Clear About Your Employment Goals If the form asks why you want to join, avoid generic answers such as: “I want to gain skills.” Instead explain: What career area you want to enter What skills you currently lack Why the programme would help you How you intend to use the training 3. Explain Your Employability Gap A strong response might identify a practical challenge such as: Limited professional experience Weak digital skills Limited workplace exposure Need for stronger communication skills Difficulty transitioning from school to employment Then explain how training could help address it. 4. Demonstrate Commitment A five-day intensive programme requires active participation. If asked about availability, applicants should ensure they can attend the full programme. Who Should Consider Applying? This opportunity may be especially relevant if you: Have recently graduated Are searching for employment Want to strengthen your practical skills Want stronger workplace readiness Live in one of the targeted regions Can commit to an intensive five-day programme Key Information at a Glance Programme: Skills Innovation Academy 2026 Country: Ghana Organizer/Implementer: GIZ Ghana Initiative: Invest for Jobs – Special Initiative “Decent Work for a Just Transition” Supporting ministry: German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ) Duration: 5 days Training focus: Technical and soft skills Purpose: Improve practical skills and employability Target participants: Graduates Regions: Greater Accra, Bono, Northern and Upper West Deadline: 23 September 2026 Application method: Online registration Application link: Skills Innovation Academy registration form The current call does not publicly state a stipend, job guarantee, accommodation package, participation allowance, age restriction or precise academic degree threshold. Conclusion The Skills Innovation Academy Ghana 2026 offers graduates in Greater Accra, Bono, Northern and Upper West an opportunity to spend five intensive days strengthening practical technical and soft skills for the workplace. The programme is part of Invest for Jobs – Special Initiative “Decent Work for a Just Transition,” supported by Germany’s BMZ and implemented by GIZ . Its emphasis is firmly on employability: helping graduates strengthen the competencies needed to transition more effectively from education into professional environments. The current call does not promise employment, a stipend or an internship. It should instead be understood as a short professional-development and skills-training opportunity. Applicants should also pay attention to the regional eligibility. The September 2026 round specifically names graduates located in Greater Accra, Bono, Northern and Upper West , and should not automatically be promoted as open to every region of Ghana. The application deadline is: 23 September 2026 Interested graduates should submit the online form as early as possible. To explore more global opportunities, VISIT HERE . title: Walter Benjamin Programme: DFG Funding for Postdoctoral Researchers to Conduct Independent Research in Germany or Abroad
summary: The Walter Benjamin Programme of the German Research Foundation, also known as the DFG , offers an important funding opportunity for postdoctoral researchers at an early stage of their academic careers who want to independently conduct their own research projects. Designed to support the transition toward an increasingly independent research career, the programme enables particularly qualified postdoctoral researchers to pursue a self-directed research project at a research institution of their choice. The project may be carried out either in Germany or abroad , depending on the applicant s circumstances and the funding module selected. The Walter Benjamin Programme places a strong emphasis on research independence, academic mobility and thematic development . By securing funding for their own project, researchers can take an important step toward establishing themselves as independent scholars while developing their research expertise, professional networks and academic careers. A key feature of the programme is that it generally requires applicants to change their research institution , reflecting the DFG s objective of encouraging mobility during the early stages of an academic research career. The funding structure differs depending on whether the project is conducted in Germany or abroad. Researchers undertaking their projects abroad may receive funding in the form of a fellowship, while projects based in Germany can be funded through a postdoctoral research position or, in some cases, a temporary substitute position. In addition to the primary funding arrangement, the programme can also provide allowances for direct project costs, travel expenses, publication costs and, where applicable, increased publication costs. For early-career postdoctoral researchers seeking to establish an independent research profile, gain experience at a new institution, conduct research internationally or strengthen their academic trajectory, the Walter Benjamin Programme represents a significant funding pathway. About the Walter Benjamin Programme The Walter Benjamin Programme is a DFG funding programme specifically designed to support researchers during the postdoctoral training and early career phase . The programme enables eligible researchers to independently conduct their own research project at a location of their choice. The chosen project may be based at a research institution in Germany or at an institution abroad, provided that the relevant eligibility and programme conditions are met. The host institution plays an important role in supporting the research project. However, applicants should carefully clarify the administrative arrangements before submitting their proposal. An important point for prospective applicants is that fellowship funding is paid exclusively to the funding recipient and is not paid into an account held by the host institution. Before submitting a proposal, applicants are therefore advised to discuss with their intended host institution whether fellowship funding can be administered in accordance with the relevant DFG regulations. This step can be particularly important for researchers planning to undertake their project at an institution outside Germany, where administrative arrangements may differ. Purpose of the Walter Benjamin Programme The central objective of the Walter Benjamin Programme is to help particularly qualified postdoctoral researchers take the next steps toward a more independent academic and research career. By obtaining funding for their own research project, researchers are given the opportunity to: Develop and pursue an independent research agenda Exercise greater autonomy in shaping their research Strengthen their academic profile Develop expertise in a particular research area Gain experience at a new research institution Expand their academic and professional networks Support their transition toward the next stages of an independent research career Develop their research interests and thematic specialization Benefit from national or international research mobility The programme recognizes that the postdoctoral phase can be a crucial period in a researcher s career. At this stage, researchers are increasingly expected to demonstrate independence, develop original research questions and establish themselves within their academic or professional field. The Walter Benjamin Programme is intended to support this process by providing researchers with the opportunity to secure funding for a project of their own. A Strong Focus on Academic Independence One of the defining features of the programme is its focus on independence. Rather than simply joining an existing research project as a team member, successful applicants receive support to pursue their own research project . This can provide postdoctoral researchers with an opportunity to demonstrate their ability to: Develop an original research proposal Define relevant research questions Plan and manage an independent project Conduct research at a host institution Produce and publish research findings Build an individual academic profile The programme is therefore particularly relevant for researchers who are moving beyond the doctoral stage and seeking to strengthen their credentials for future academic, research or other professional opportunities. Research Location: Germany or Abroad A major feature of the Walter Benjamin Programme is the flexibility to conduct the research project either in Germany or abroad . Applicants can select a suitable research institution based on the requirements of their proposed project and their academic or professional development. However, the funding structure and eligibility conditions can differ depending on where the project will be conducted. Conducting the Project in Germany Researchers carrying out their project in Germany may receive funding through a position under the staff category: Postdoctoral researcher and comparable In certain cases, a temporary substitute position may also be funded, usually under the staff category: Medical research assistant The host institution and host researchers are expected to provide appropriate support for the implementation of the project and the researcher s career development. This means that the programme is not solely focused on financing the individual researcher. The institutional environment and support provided to the researcher are also relevant to the successful implementation of the project. Conducting the Project Abroad For projects conducted abroad, funding is provided in the form of a fellowship . Researchers considering an international research stay should carefully review the special eligibility provisions that apply to Walter Benjamin fellowships abroad. These provisions include requirements related to the applicant s integration into Germany s academic research system, previous research activity, educational background and the amount of time already spent abroad for research purposes. Special Eligibility Provisions for Walter Benjamin Fellowships Abroad Funding for research abroad is subject to specific conditions. The programme states that funding abroad can be provided when researchers are integrated into Germany s academic research system. This integration may be demonstrated in different ways depending on the applicant s current location and academic background. Researchers Based in Germany Before Applying Researchers may be considered integrated into Germany s academic research system if, immediately before submitting their proposal, they have worked as a researcher in Germany for a continuous period of at least three years during their doctoral and/or postdoctoral phase. This requirement is particularly important for applicants who want to use the Walter Benjamin Programme to move from a German research environment to a host institution abroad. Researchers Already Based Abroad Researchers who are already based outside Germany may also be eligible for funding abroad under certain circumstances. According to the programme conditions, funding can be provided if the researcher: Has completed the majority of their schooling and higher education in Germany; and Has not spent more than three years abroad for research purposes as of the time of proposal submission after completing their doctorate in Germany or abroad. These provisions mean that researchers currently living or working outside Germany should carefully assess their educational and research history before applying. Previous Time at the Proposed Host Institution Another important requirement concerns the applicant s previous employment or research activity at the institution chosen as the host for the Walter Benjamin fellowship. At the time of proposal submission, applicants must not have worked for longer than one year at the selected host institution. This condition is consistent with the programme s broader objective of promoting research mobility and encouraging researchers to change their institutional environment. Research Mobility as a Key Objective The Walter Benjamin Programme specifically aims to promote mobility during the early stages of a research career. For this reason, the programme generally requires the applicant to change their research institution . Academic mobility can provide researchers with opportunities to: Work in a new institutional environment Establish new collaborations Access different research resources Develop international or national research networks Learn new methodologies Gain exposure to new academic perspectives Expand the scope of their research Build a more independent professional profile Researchers should therefore consider the mobility requirement carefully when identifying a host institution and developing their research proposal. Restrictions on the Type of Host Institution The proposed research project may not be based at an entity that: Is for-profit; or Does not permit the publication of research findings in a generally accessible form This requirement reflects the academic and research-oriented purpose of the programme. Applicants should therefore ensure that their proposed host institution provides an appropriate environment for independent research and allows research findings to be made publicly accessible. Type and Extent of Funding The exact type and extent of funding available through the Walter Benjamin Programme depends on the funding module selected and whether the project is carried out in Germany or abroad. Funding for Research Abroad For projects conducted abroad, funding is provided as a fellowship. The fellowship includes a monthly basic amount and may also include additional allowances where applicable. These may include: Foreign allowances Cost-of-living allowance Travel allowance Benefits for fellowship recipients with children The availability and amount of funding depend on the relevant programme provisions and the applicant s individual circumstances. The DFG also provides an Award Calculator that researchers can use to estimate the level of funding they may receive. Funding for Research in Germany For projects based in Germany, funding is generally provided through a position under the staff category of: Postdoctoral researcher and comparable In certain circumstances, a temporary substitute position may also be available, usually under the category of medical research assistant. Combining Funding Modules The programme also allows the possibility of combining funding arrangements. This can provide flexibility for researchers whose proposed project includes different phases or research locations. Applicants should carefully consider which module or combination of modules is most appropriate for their proposed research project and career development. Additional Funding and Project Costs Regardless of the funding module selected, the programme provides for allowances relating to important research and project expenses. These can include: Direct project costs Travel expenses Publication costs Increased publication costs where applicable, including literature-related costs These additional forms of support can be important because research projects often involve expenses beyond the basic funding provided to support the researcher. Applicants should therefore carefully examine the forms, guidelines and programme documentation when preparing their proposal and research budget. Support for Researchers With Children Where applicable, the fellowship can also provide benefits for fellowship recipients with children. This is one of the additional components included within the fellowship structure, alongside the monthly basic amount and possible allowances for foreign living costs and travel. Applicants with children should review the applicable DFG funding regulations and programme guidance to understand which benefits may apply to their individual circumstances. Funding Duration The Walter Benjamin Programme provides funding for a period of up to two years as a rule . This duration can give postdoctoral researchers a substantial period in which to: Develop their research project Conduct research Build new collaborations Develop methodological expertise Work within a new research environment Produce academic outputs Strengthen their independent academic profile Prepare for the next stage of their research career The two-year funding period can therefore offer researchers a structured period of support during a critical phase of career development. Important Requirements Before Submitting a Proposal Prospective applicants should not wait until their proposal is fully prepared before communicating with the intended host institution. The programme specifically advises applicants to clarify whether the fellowship funding can be administered by the host institution in accordance with DFG regulations. Applicants should therefore consider discussing the following with their proposed host institution: Whether the institution is willing to host the proposed research project Whether the institution can provide the necessary support for the project Whether the fellowship funding arrangements can be administered in accordance with DFG regulations Whether the proposed research environment is suitable for the project Whether the institution permits research findings to be published in a generally accessible form Whether the applicant satisfies the programme s mobility and previous-employment requirements These discussions can help applicants avoid administrative difficulties after investing substantial time in preparing a proposal. Special Note for Researchers Planning a Fellowship in France The programme provides a specific note for applicants planning a postdoctoral fellowship at a research institution in France. According to the information provided, French legislation allows postdoctoral fellowships at research institutions in France for a maximum period of 12 months . However, enquiries with the French Ministry of Higher Education, Research and Innovation have indicated that fellowships may be granted for a period of up to 24 months if the postdoctoral researcher moves to another institution in France after 12 months. Researchers planning a stay in France under the Walter Benjamin Programme should take this requirement into account while developing their proposal. Where applicable, both host institutions must already have been confirmed at the time the proposal is submitted. This means applicants considering a two-year research period in France may need to: Plan for a change of host institution after the first 12 months Identify both institutions in advance Confirm the willingness of both institutions to host the researcher Ensure that the research plan is structured appropriately Have both institutions confirmed at the time of proposal submission where required Researchers considering this option should pay particular attention to the administrative and planning implications before submitting their proposal. Who Is Eligible for the Walter Benjamin Programme? The programme is specifically aimed at postdoctoral researchers at an early career stage . Applicants should therefore be in the postdoctoral phase of their research career and seeking to develop greater independence through their own research project. The programme is intended for particularly qualified researchers who are ready to take the next steps toward an increasingly autonomous academic or research career. Depending on the location of the proposed research project, additional eligibility requirements may apply. Applicants planning research abroad must pay particular attention to the requirements concerning: Integration into Germany s academic research system Previous research activity in Germany Educational history Time spent abroad for research purposes Previous work at the proposed host institution How to Prepare a Strong Walter Benjamin Programme Proposal Preparing a proposal for an independent research funding programme requires careful planning. Although the programme information emphasizes the applicant s own research project, independence and mobility, applicants should ensure that their proposal clearly demonstrates the significance and feasibility of the proposed work. A strong preparation process may involve the following steps. 1. Define an Independent Research Project Applicants should clearly establish the research question, objectives and expected direction of their proposed project. Because the programme supports the applicant s own research project, it is important that the proposal reflects an independent and clearly defined research agenda. 2. Select an Appropriate Host Institution The host institution should provide an appropriate environment for carrying out the research. Applicants should consider factors such as: Research expertise Available facilities and resources Potential academic collaborations Institutional support Compatibility with the proposed research Publication requirements Administrative arrangements 3. Check the Mobility Requirement Because the programme generally requires applicants to change their research institution, researchers should carefully examine whether their proposed host institution meets this requirement. Applicants for fellowships abroad should also ensure that they have not worked at the selected host institution for longer than one year at the time of proposal submission. 4. Review Eligibility for Research Abroad Applicants planning to conduct their project outside Germany should carefully review the additional eligibility requirements. Their academic and research history may be particularly important in determining whether they are considered integrated into Germany s academic research system. 5. Discuss Administrative Arrangements With the Host Institution Before submitting the proposal, applicants should clarify whether the host institution can administer fellowship funding in accordance with DFG regulations. This is an important practical step because the fellowship is paid directly to the funding recipient rather than into an institutional account. 6. Plan the Funding Structure Applicants should consider whether their project will be based: Entirely in Germany Entirely abroad Through a combination of funding modules or locations The selected structure should support both the research project and the applicant s career development. 7. Consider Project-Related Expenses Applicants should review the potential costs associated with: Research activities Travel Publications Literature and increased publication costs where applicable The programme provides allowances for several of these areas, subject to the relevant funding rules. Apply here Forms, Guidelines and Proposal Documentation The DFG provides forms, templates and additional guidelines for the Walter Benjamin Programme. Prospective applicants should carefully review the official programme documentation before preparing and submitting a proposal. The available materials can help researchers understand: Programme requirements Funding conditions Proposal preparation Relevant forms Supporting documentation Administrative procedures Applicants should ensure that they are using the relevant and current documentation for their application. Proposal Deadline: Is There a Fixed Deadline? Based on the information provided, a section titled “Proposal Deadlines” is listed for the Walter Benjamin Programme, but no specific application or proposal deadline date is stated in the supplied information . Therefore, applicants should not assume a particular deadline from this programme description alone. Prospective applicants should check the relevant official DFG proposal deadline information and current programme guidance before planning their submission. This is particularly important because funding opportunities and proposal procedures may have specific submission requirements or schedules. Additional Information and Support The programme information also provides access to additional resources related to research careers and the Walter Benjamin Programme. These include: Forms and guidelines Frequently asked questions Further programme information A downloadable Walter Benjamin Programme flyer Information on how the DFG supports research careers Information talks on DFG funding opportunities for research careers A discussion platform for fellows abroad Information relating to refugee researchers Videos explaining the programme and the researchers supported through DFG funding The available videos include material explaining: Who can apply for funding Funding conditions The process of preparing a proposal Experiences and perspectives of DFG-funded researchers The research being conducted by funded researchers These resources may be particularly useful for first-time applicants who want to better understand the expectations associated with independent research funding. Why the Walter Benjamin Programme Can Be Important for Early-Career Researchers The transition from doctoral research to an independent research career can be one of the most significant stages in an academic career. During this period, researchers may need to demonstrate that they can: Develop their own research agenda Secure competitive funding Build professional networks Work independently Establish expertise in a specialized area Adapt to new research environments Develop an increasingly autonomous academic profile The Walter Benjamin Programme is designed to support researchers during this transition. Its focus on independent research funding, institutional mobility and career development can make it particularly relevant for postdoctoral researchers seeking to establish the foundations for future academic or research opportunities. The possibility of conducting research in Germany or abroad also provides researchers with flexibility in identifying an environment that best supports their project. For more details visit here Key Features of the Walter Benjamin Programme at a Glance The main features of the programme include: Funding for early-career postdoctoral researchers Support for an independently developed research project Research opportunities in Germany or abroad A strong emphasis on academic independence A general requirement to change the research institution Funding for up to two years as a rule Fellowship funding for research projects conducted abroad Postdoctoral research positions for projects conducted in Germany Possible combination of funding modules Monthly basic fellowship funding Possible foreign allowances Possible cost-of-living allowance Travel allowance Benefits for eligible fellowship recipients with children Allowances for direct project costs Support for travel expenses Support for publication costs Possible increased publication costs Special eligibility provisions for research projects abroad Specific guidance for researchers planning a fellowship in France Host institution support for the research project and career development Conclusion The DFG Walter Benjamin Programme provides a significant opportunity for early-career postdoctoral researchers who want to take greater control of their research trajectory and conduct an independent research project in Germany or abroad. By supporting researchers during the postdoctoral phase, the programme aims to help them develop the autonomy, mobility and thematic expertise needed for the next stages of an increasingly independent research career. The programme s flexible structure allows projects to be conducted at research institutions in Germany or internationally, although applicants must carefully consider the different funding arrangements and eligibility requirements that apply to each option. Researchers planning a project abroad should pay particular attention to the additional conditions relating to their connection with Germany s academic research system, the amount of time previously spent abroad and the period already spent at the proposed host institution. Funding is generally available for up to two years and may include a combination of a monthly basic amount, relevant allowances, travel support, publication costs and other project-related expenses, depending on the selected funding module and individual circumstances. Applicants should begin preparing early by developing a strong independent research project, identifying a suitable host institution, confirming the relevant administrative arrangements and carefully reviewing the DFG s current forms and guidelines. For postdoctoral researchers seeking to strengthen their academic independence, gain experience at a new institution, develop their own research profile and prepare for the next stage of their research career, the Walter Benjamin Programme can provide an important pathway toward greater academic and professional autonomy. Before submitting a proposal, applicants should verify the current proposal submission requirements and deadlines through the relevant official DFG programme information, as no specific deadline date is provided in the information supplied here. title: U.S. Treasury International Affairs Junior Fellowship 2027–2029: Paid Two-Year Opportunity for Recent College Graduates in International
summary: The U.S. Department of the Treasury is recruiting candidates for its International Affairs Junior Fellowship 2027–2029 , a highly selective, fixed two-year program designed for new college graduates interested in international economic policy, finance, public policy, international relations, and related fields. The fellowship provides an opportunity to work within Treasury’s Office of International Affairs (IA) and contribute to issues that shape U.S. international economic policy. Junior Fellows can gain exposure to international financial and economic developments, policy analysis, government decision-making, and bilateral and multilateral engagement involving major international institutions and forums. Unlike a conventional entry-level position focused on a single function, the Junior Fellowship is structured to provide fellows with exposure to multiple policy issues and opportunities to develop practical analytical, policy, and professional skills. Fellows may contribute to policy proposals, analytical studies, international economic and financial analysis, and preparations for high-level meetings involving organizations and forums such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF), World Bank, G7, and G20 . The program is particularly relevant for recent undergraduate graduates who want to build careers in government, international economic policy, public policy, international relations, finance, or related areas. Application deadline: October 31, 2026 About the U.S. Treasury International Affairs Junior Fellowship The International Affairs Junior Fellowship is a highly selective, two-year program within the U.S. Department of the Treasury s Office of International Affairs. The program is designed specifically for new college graduates and offers fellows the opportunity to gain firsthand experience in the development and implementation of international economic policy for the United States. During the two-year appointment, Junior Fellows can expect to work on a variety of assignments and policy questions rather than being limited to one narrow area of responsibility. This can include examining international economic and financial developments, developing policy proposals, conducting analytical research, and supporting senior Treasury officials in international engagements. The program can therefore serve as a strong early-career pathway for graduates who want to understand how international economic policy is developed within the U.S. government. According to the program description, previous fellows have gone on to pursue diverse career and academic paths, including: Employment with the U.S. Department of the Treasury Other positions within the U.S. government Careers in the private sector Graduate education Law Public policy International relations Finance and business This makes the fellowship potentially valuable not only as a two-year professional experience but also as a foundation for longer-term careers in international affairs and economic policy. What Do International Affairs Junior Fellows Do? Junior Fellows are exposed to multiple policy issues and are given opportunities to strengthen their knowledge and professional capabilities through practical work. Their responsibilities typically include several areas of policy and analytical work. 1. Developing Policy Proposals Fellows may contribute to the development of policy proposals relating to international economic and financial issues. This can involve understanding a policy problem, reviewing relevant information and developments, analyzing potential approaches, and contributing to recommendations or proposals for consideration by Treasury officials. For graduates interested in public policy, this provides exposure to how policy ideas are developed in a major U.S. government department. 2. Analyzing International Economic and Financial Developments Another important component of the fellowship is monitoring and analyzing international economic and financial developments. This may require fellows to follow developments affecting international economies and financial systems and assess their implications for U.S. economic policy and international engagement. Such experience can be particularly relevant for individuals interested in: International economics Global finance Macroeconomic policy Financial policy International development Global economic relations Public policy 3. Conducting Analytical Studies Junior Fellows may also conduct analytical studies as part of their responsibilities. This gives participants an opportunity to apply academic knowledge to real-world policy questions and develop skills in research, analysis, evidence assessment, and policy-oriented writing. 4. Supporting Bilateral and Multilateral Meetings Fellows can support bilateral and multilateral meetings involving senior Treasury officials. The program specifically highlights engagements involving major international institutions and forums, including: International Monetary Fund (IMF) World Bank G7 G20 Junior Fellows often participate in these meetings and may have opportunities to travel abroad. This component can provide valuable exposure to international economic diplomacy and the practical processes involved in high-level government engagement. Where Are Junior Fellows Placed? Junior Fellows are placed in either a regional office or a functional office within Treasury s Office of International Affairs. The two types of offices provide exposure to different aspects of international economic policy. Regional Offices Regional offices oversee Treasury s engagement with counterpart finance ministries and treasuries around the world. Working in a regional office can therefore provide exposure to U.S. economic relationships with specific countries or regions and the policy issues associated with those relationships. Depending on their assignment, fellows may gain experience understanding: International economic relationships Government-to-government engagement Economic policy developments in other countries Regional economic issues Engagement with foreign finance ministries and treasuries Bilateral policy discussions Functional Offices Functional offices focus on engagement with international financial institutions and broader Treasury policy issues. The program identifies areas including: International financial institutions International trade Export credits Foreign exchange Functional assignments can therefore provide fellows with exposure to policy questions that extend across individual countries or regions. A Unique Opportunity to Work in International Economic Policy For graduates interested in international affairs, the fellowship provides an opportunity to move beyond classroom learning and gain practical experience in U.S. international economic policy. The program sits at the intersection of several disciplines, including: Economics Finance International relations Public policy International economic policy Government Global financial affairs This multidisciplinary nature means that candidates do not necessarily need to pursue a narrowly defined career path within economics. Applicants with relevant academic preparation and interests in related policy fields may also be well positioned for the program. International Exposure and Potential Travel One of the distinctive aspects of the Junior Fellowship is the opportunity to engage with international issues and, potentially, international meetings. The program states that Junior Fellows may participate in meetings involving international institutions and major multilateral forums and may have opportunities to travel abroad . However, international travel should not be understood as an automatic component of every fellow s experience. The opportunity will depend on the fellow s office, duties, assignments, and program requirements. The international exposure can nevertheless be particularly valuable for graduates seeking careers in: International organizations Government Diplomacy International development Global finance Economic policy International relations Who Should Consider Applying? The program is particularly suited to recent college graduates who are interested in understanding and contributing to international economic policy. Strong candidates may have academic backgrounds or relevant coursework in: Economics Public policy Finance International relations Related fields The Treasury specifically notes that strong candidates will have recently received, or will soon receive, a bachelor s degree with relevant coursework in these areas. The program also states that, because of its structure, preference is given to undergraduates . International Affairs Junior Fellowship Eligibility and Qualifications The formal qualifications are particularly important for applicants to understand before preparing an application. Candidates should meet the following key requirements. Bachelor s Degree Candidates should have recently received, or be close to receiving, a bachelor s degree . Relevant coursework may include: Economics Public policy Finance International relations Related disciplines Preference for Undergraduates The program explicitly states that preference is given to undergraduates because of the structure of the Junior Fellowship. This means candidates should carefully consider how their educational stage aligns with the program before applying. Relevant Experience Applicants must also demonstrate 52 weeks, or 2,080 hours, of relevant paid or unpaid experience . Importantly, this experience does not have to come exclusively from conventional employment. The application instructions specifically allow relevant experience to include: Paid employment Unpaid work Volunteer experience Extracurricular activities Work-study experience Other professional or extracurricular activities relevant to the duties described by the program This makes it important for applicants to review their entire background rather than considering only formal full-time jobs. How to Document the Required 52 Weeks of Experience One of the most important aspects of the application is demonstrating the required 52 weeks (2,080 hours) of relevant experience. Applicants are instructed to provide sufficient detail in their resumes to demonstrate this experience. The resume should explain the duties performed in each relevant professional or extracurricular activity. Candidates should include: The position or activity The organization or setting The period during which the activity took place The number of hours per week The duties performed How the duties relate to the fellowship For example, the application guidance gives the format of specifying dates and weekly hours, such as: June 1, 2025 to August 31, 2025, 30 hours per week Applicants should therefore avoid simply listing an organization and job title without describing what they actually did. The purpose is to make it possible for reviewers to determine whether the applicant has the relevant experience required by the program. Resume Requirements The Treasury provides specific instructions regarding the resume. Maximum Length: Two Pages The resume should not exceed two pages . This is particularly important because candidates need to demonstrate the required 52 weeks of experience while remaining within the two-page limit. Applicants should therefore prioritize: Relevant responsibilities Analytical experience Policy-related activities Research International affairs exposure Economics or finance-related experience Public policy experience Government or nonprofit experience Relevant volunteer activities Relevant extracurricular activities Rather than merely listing responsibilities, candidates should explain the work they performed and demonstrate its relevance to the Junior Fellowship. Application Documents Required Candidates must submit several materials by email. The application package should include: Cover letter Resume One recommendation letter Transcript(s) demonstrating academic qualifications and career potential These documents should be sent to: IAFellows@treasury.gov The application deadline is October 31, 2026 . Additional Information Required in the Application Email In addition to submitting the required documents, candidates must provide specific information in their application email. Applicants must: 1. Indicate Their Desired Start Date Candidates should state when they would ideally like to begin the fellowship. 2. Confirm U.S. Citizenship Candidates must confirm that they hold U.S. citizenship and must be able to provide documentation proving their citizenship. 3. Note Veterans Preference Candidates should indicate whether they are eligible for veterans preference, if applicable. 4. Demonstrate the Required Experience The submitted resume must demonstrate the required 52 weeks (2,080 hours) of relevant paid or unpaid work, volunteer, or extracurricular experience. What Happens After You Apply? The selection process does not end with submission of the initial application. Candidates who pass the first round of screening will be asked to respond to two short essay questions . This means applicants should be prepared to demonstrate not only their academic and professional qualifications but also their ability to communicate clearly about their interests, experiences, and suitability for the fellowship. The application materials are expected to be evaluated in December 2026 . Selected Fellows are expected to begin in summer 2027 , although an alternative start time may be mutually agreed upon. International Affairs Junior Fellowship Timeline The key timeline for the 2027–2029 recruitment cycle is: Stage Timeline Application deadline October 31, 2026 Application evaluation December 2026 Fellowship begins Summer 2027 Program duration Two years Expected program period 2027–2029 Candidates should not wait until the final day to assemble their materials because the application requires multiple documents, including a recommendation letter and transcript(s). National Security Clearance Requirement An important condition of the fellowship is that candidates must be able to obtain and maintain a national security clearance . This requirement should be taken seriously by applicants. A candidate may meet the educational and experience requirements but still need to satisfy the applicable security-clearance requirements to participate in the program. Applicants should therefore understand that selection for the fellowship is not necessarily the only consideration in determining eligibility to serve in the position. Salary and Employment Benefits Junior Fellows are usually hired at the GS-9 level and receive standard Treasury benefits. This makes the program distinct from unpaid academic fellowships or many short-term graduate programs. The fellowship combines: A two-year professional appointment Work within the U.S. Department of the Treasury International economic policy exposure Potential international travel Professional development Standard Treasury benefits Experience working with senior officials and international counterparts For recent graduates, this combination can provide substantial exposure to public-sector economic policymaking. Career Opportunities After the Fellowship The fellowship can provide a strong foundation for a range of future career paths. According to the Treasury s description, former fellows have pursued opportunities including employment at Treasury, other U.S. government positions, private-sector careers, and graduate education. Potential longer-term directions include: U.S. government careers International economic policy Public policy International relations Finance Business Law Graduate study International affairs Economic analysis The fellowship can therefore be viewed as an early-career platform for graduates who want to build expertise in international economic and financial policy. Apply here Information Sessions for Prospective Applicants The Junior Fellows recruiting committee plans to host three information sessions before the application deadline. These sessions are intended to help prospective applicants better understand the program and hear directly from current fellows. The sessions will be led by current Junior Fellows from different International Affairs offices. Participants will have an opportunity to: Ask questions about the Junior Fellowship Hear about current fellows experiences Learn more about working in Treasury International Affairs Gain insight into the fellowship from people currently participating in the program The Treasury states that date and registration information for these sessions will be available on the relevant page in late summer 2026. Why the Information Sessions Could Be Valuable Prospective applicants should consider attending the information sessions if possible. Because the Junior Fellowship is highly selective, understanding the program from current fellows can help candidates gain a clearer picture of: The nature of the work Different International Affairs offices The experience of working at Treasury Potential responsibilities The transition from college to government policy work The expectations associated with the fellowship Candidates can also use the opportunity to ask questions before submitting their applications. How to Prepare a Strong Application Although the Treasury sets out the formal application requirements, applicants can strengthen their preparation by making sure every document clearly demonstrates relevance to the fellowship. 1. Tailor Your Resume to International Affairs A generic graduate resume may not effectively communicate your suitability. Focus on experiences involving: Economic analysis Research Policy Finance International affairs Government Public-sector work Data analysis Writing International organizations Development Volunteer activities Relevant extracurricular activities 2. Clearly Demonstrate the 2,080-Hour Requirement Do not make the reviewer calculate your experience themselves. Where appropriate, clearly state: Start and end dates Hours per week Position/activity Responsibilities This is especially important for candidates whose experience is spread across internships, volunteering, extracurricular activities, part-time employment, or work-study. 3. Keep the Resume Within Two Pages The two-page requirement means candidates need to be selective. Prioritize experiences that demonstrate capabilities relevant to the responsibilities of an International Affairs Junior Fellow. 4. Make the Cover Letter Specific The cover letter should explain why the applicant is interested in: International economic policy The U.S. Department of the Treasury International Affairs The Junior Fellowship The specific skills and experiences they bring A generic statement about wanting a government job is unlikely to communicate the same level of fit as a carefully targeted application. 5. Prepare for the Essay Stage Candidates who pass the initial screening will be asked to answer two short essay questions. Applicants should therefore be prepared to discuss their: Academic background Professional experience Policy interests Analytical skills International interests Motivation for joining Treasury Career goals For more details please visit here What Makes This Fellowship Different? Several features distinguish the International Affairs Junior Fellowship from a typical graduate recruitment opportunity. Two-Year Structure The fellowship is a fixed two-year program , providing more time for fellows to develop substantive professional expertise than a short internship. International Economic Policy Focus The program is specifically focused on international economic policy, making it highly relevant to graduates interested in global economic affairs. Exposure to Major International Institutions Fellows may support meetings involving organizations and forums such as the IMF, World Bank, G7, and G20. Regional and Functional Career Exposure Fellows can be placed in either regional or functional offices, exposing them to different dimensions of international policy. Potential International Travel Junior Fellows may have opportunities to participate in meetings and travel abroad depending on their assignments. Government Experience The program provides direct experience within the U.S. Department of the Treasury. Potential Long-Term Career Pathways Former fellows have gone on to careers in Treasury, elsewhere in the U.S. government, the private sector, and graduate education. Frequently Asked Questions What is the International Affairs Junior Fellowship? It is a highly selective, fixed two-year program within the U.S. Department of the Treasury s Office of International Affairs for new college graduates interested in international economic policy. How long is the Junior Fellowship? The program lasts two years , with the current recruitment cycle covering 2027–2029 . When is the application deadline? The application deadline is October 31, 2026 . When will the selected Fellows begin? Fellows are expected to begin in summer 2027 , although an alternative start time may be mutually agreed upon. What degree is required? Strong candidates will have recently received, or will soon receive, a bachelor s degree with relevant coursework. What subjects are relevant? The Treasury identifies economics, public policy, finance, international relations, and related fields. Is preference given to undergraduate students? Yes. The program specifically states that preference is given to undergraduates due to the structure of the program. Is previous work experience required? Candidates must demonstrate 52 weeks (2,080 hours) of relevant paid or unpaid work, volunteer, or extracurricular experience. Can volunteer or extracurricular experience count? Yes. The application instructions specifically allow relevant paid or unpaid work, volunteer, and extracurricular experience. How long can the resume be? The resume should not exceed two pages . Is U.S. citizenship required? Yes. Candidates must confirm that they hold U.S. citizenship and must be able to provide documentation. Is a security clearance required? Candidates must be able to obtain and maintain a national security clearance . Are Fellows paid? Junior Fellows are usually hired at the GS-9 level and receive standard Treasury benefits. Can Fellows travel internationally? Junior Fellows may have opportunities to travel abroad, depending on their work and assignments. Will there be interviews or additional selection steps? Candidates who pass the first screening stage will be asked to respond to two short essay questions . When are applications evaluated? The applications are expected to be evaluated in December 2026 . Where should applications be submitted? Applications should be emailed to IAFellows@treasury.gov . Application Checklist Before submitting an application, prospective candidates should ensure they have: A cover letter A resume of no more than two pages One recommendation letter Transcript(s) Evidence of the required 52 weeks/2,080 hours of relevant experience Desired start date included in the email Confirmation of U.S. citizenship Veterans preference information, if applicable Detailed descriptions of relevant duties and activities Dates and weekly hours for relevant experiences Prepared for the possibility of two short essay questions Considered their ability to obtain and maintain a national security clearance Important Deadline The deadline to apply for the U.S. Treasury International Affairs Junior Fellowship 2027–2029 is: October 31, 2026 Applicants should prepare their recommendation letter, transcripts, resume, and cover letter well before the deadline. The requirement to document 52 weeks or 2,080 hours of relevant experience also means candidates should carefully review their past work, volunteer, and extracurricular activities before submitting their application. Conclusion The U.S. Department of the Treasury International Affairs Junior Fellowship 2027–2029 offers recent college graduates an opportunity to begin a career in international economic policy through a structured, two-year professional program. The fellowship combines analytical work, policy development, international economic research, and exposure to bilateral and multilateral engagements. Junior Fellows may work in regional or functional offices and can gain experience with issues involving international financial institutions, trade, export credits, foreign exchange, and international economic relationships. The opportunity is particularly relevant for graduates with backgrounds in economics, public policy, finance, international relations, or related fields who want to develop careers in government, international affairs, public policy, finance, or global economic policy. With placements within the U.S. Treasury s Office of International Affairs, potential exposure to institutions such as the IMF and World Bank and forums such as the G7 and G20, and the possibility of international travel, the program can provide substantial early-career exposure to international policymaking. Candidates should pay close attention to the specific application requirements, particularly the two-page resume limit, 52-week/2,080-hour experience requirement, U.S. citizenship requirement, recommendation letter, transcripts, and national security clearance requirement . For eligible applicants, this is an opportunity to gain meaningful professional experience at one of the United States key economic policy institutions while building a foundation for future careers in government, international relations, finance, public policy, or further graduate study.
