title: IBRO Seeding Neuroscience Grants 2026: Funding for New Neuroscience Societies and Thematic Networks in Africa, Asia-Pacific and Latin America
summary: Applications are now open for the IBRO Seeding Neuroscience Grants 2026 , an international funding opportunity designed to help groups of scientists and organizations take the first practical steps toward establishing sustainable neuroscience societies, sub-societies, regional chapters and thematic research networks. Offered by the International Brain Research Organization (IBRO) , the programme focuses specifically on regions where stronger formal structures for neuroscience collaboration could expand scientific exchange, professional networking, representation and long-term research capacity. Applications are open to eligible initiatives in: Africa Asia-Pacific Latin America The 2026 application window runs from: 1 September 2026 to 30 September 2026 The application deadline is therefore: 30 September 2026 Applications must be submitted through the official IBRO Grants Portal . Apply for the IBRO Seeding Neuroscience Grants Read the official programme information About the IBRO Seeding Neuroscience Grants The IBRO Seeding Neuroscience Grants are intended to provide early-stage financial support for scientists who want to create stronger and more formal neuroscience communities. The programme recognizes that in some countries or regions, neuroscientists may already be collaborating informally but lack: A formal professional society An organizational structure Governance arrangements A sustainable membership system A dedicated regional chapter A network focused on a particular neuroscience discipline IBRO therefore provides funding for the inaugural activities needed to move from informal scientific collaboration toward a formal, sustainable structure . This can include activities such as: Governance planning Strategic workshops Organizational development Discussions on leadership and membership Planning the structure of a new neuroscience society Developing a thematic scientific network Establishing a regional or sub-national neuroscience chapter The central purpose is not simply to organize another scientific event. Instead, the funding should help scientists create something that continues beyond the initial funded activity. What Is the Main Aim of the Programme? The official aim of the programme is to: Support the development of emerging neuroscience societies or thematic networks. IBRO wants to empower local neuroscientists and organizations to come together, establish common objectives and build the governance structures necessary for a sustainable scientific community. The programme can therefore support initiatives that lead to the creation of: National neuroscience societies Regional neuroscience societies Formal neuroscience sub-societies Regional chapters Thematic neuroscience networks The programme is particularly valuable where researchers are already interested in building a collaborative community but lack the financial resources needed to organize the planning process. What Types of Neuroscience Communities Can Be Created? The programme is broader than the establishment of a traditional national neuroscience society. Applicants may also propose a formal community focused on a specific neuroscience field. IBRO gives examples such as: Computational neuroscience Glial research Other thematic networks may potentially fit the programme where they represent a genuine unmet need and are consistent with the call requirements. A thematic network could be useful where researchers in a specialized field are spread across several institutions or countries but do not yet have a recognized body through which to: Coordinate activities Build research collaborations Support early-career scientists Share resources Organize training Advocate for their research field Develop regional scientific capacity Who Can Apply? IBRO welcomes applications from: Emerging Neuroscience Societies Groups that already function informally as a neuroscience community but have not yet become a formally established society may apply. Groups of Scientists A group of researchers actively planning to form a neuroscience society, chapter, sub-society or thematic network may submit an application. Scientific Organizations Organizations representing the interests of the neuroscience community may also apply where their proposed activities are directed toward establishing a formal neuroscience structure. Groups in Regions With Limited Neuroscience Infrastructure The programme particularly fits areas where there is: Little formal neuroscience organization Limited opportunity for scientific exchange No functioning neuroscience society Limited representation of a specific neuroscience discipline Applicants With a Concrete Establishment Plan Applicants should have a clear and actionable plan for moving from the initial funded activity to an actual formal society or network. This is crucial. IBRO is not looking simply for groups that say they may eventually form an organization. The proposal should demonstrate that the funded activities are part of a genuine process toward establishment. Geographic Eligibility The programme is open in three broad regions: Africa Groups of neuroscientists and eligible organizations based in African countries may apply where they meet the programme criteria. Asia-Pacific Eligible scientific groups and organizations from the Asia-Pacific region may also participate. Latin America The programme is additionally open to qualifying initiatives based in Latin America. The official programme information provided does not list a single closed country-by-country eligibility table in the text supplied. Applicants should therefore check the IBRO Grants Portal or contact the IBRO programmes team if there is any uncertainty about whether their location falls within the relevant IBRO regional structure. What if a National Neuroscience Society Already Exists? The existence of an established national neuroscience society does not automatically prevent an application, but the rules become significantly more restrictive. In countries where a national neuroscience society already exists, including an IBRO member society , applicants may apply only where they are formally seeking to establish something distinct, such as: A neuroscience sub-society A specialized thematic body A regional chapter The proposed activity must focus on the planning and governance required to launch that new structure. Applicants must also demonstrate that the proposed organization provides clear added value . For example, it could address: An underserved geographic area A specialized neuroscience subfield A group of scientists not adequately represented by the existing society A particular scientific or professional need that the national organization does not currently meet Creating a duplicate organization without a convincing reason is unlikely to fit the purpose of the programme. A New Society Must Address an Unmet Need Where an existing neuroscience society already operates, applicants should clearly explain: What is missing from the existing scientific ecosystem Which researchers are underserved Why a new sub-society or regional chapter is needed How the proposed group complements rather than competes unnecessarily with the existing organization What scientific or regional value the new structure will add This is particularly important for thematic groups. For example, if a national neuroscience society exists but there is no organized community for computational neuroscience, a proposal to create a formal computational neuroscience network may be relevant if the applicants can demonstrate a real scientific need. What Activities Can the Grant Support? The programme is intended for inaugural and organizational activities that directly contribute to the creation of a sustainable neuroscience body. Examples can include: Governance Planning Applicants may organize activities to determine: Organizational structure Leadership arrangements Executive roles Decision-making procedures Membership models Constitutions or bylaws Internal governance processes Governance is central because a sustainable professional society needs more than an informal network of scientists. Strategic Workshops A funded planning workshop could bring together researchers to decide: The mission of the new society Scientific priorities Membership strategy Leadership model Future activities Regional representation Funding plans Diversity and inclusion commitments The workshop should produce a practical outcome rather than ending simply as a discussion event. Community-Building Activities Early activities may also help identify and connect neuroscientists who could become founding members. This could involve: Mapping researchers Creating institutional links Engaging universities Developing communication structures Establishing working groups The ultimate goal should still be the formal establishment of a society or network. Standalone Conferences Are Not Eligible One of the most important restrictions is that the Seeding Neuroscience Grants are not ordinary conference grants . IBRO explicitly states that the programme: Does not support standalone conferences or scientific meetings where the sole purpose is event organization. This means applicants should not submit a proposal simply to fund: A symposium Scientific congress Research conference Workshop with no follow-up structure Academic meeting unrelated to formal organization-building An event may form part of the proposal, but it must be tied to a clear and actionable plan to establish a: Society Sub-society Regional chapter Thematic network The organizational outcome must be central. Example of an Eligible Approach Imagine neuroscientists from several universities in one country have never had a national professional society. They could propose a planning workshop bringing together representatives from universities, research institutes and hospitals. The workshop might focus on: Agreeing on a constitution Electing an interim steering group Defining membership rules Identifying scientific priorities Developing a two-year strategic plan Agreeing on registration procedures If the outcome is a concrete pathway toward establishing a recognized national neuroscience society, that would align much more closely with the programme than simply holding a research conference. Example of a Weak Proposal A group proposes a two-day neuroscience symposium with: Keynote speakers Poster sessions Scientific presentations Networking but provides no real plan for creating a continuing organization afterward. Even if the conference is scientifically strong, it would not meet the fundamental purpose of the Seeding Neuroscience Grants. The programme is about institution-building , not simply event delivery. Building Sustainable Neuroscience Communities Sustainability is an important underlying principle of this funding opportunity. IBRO wants the initial grant to help create a neuroscience community that can continue functioning after the funded activities end. Applicants should therefore think beyond the first workshop. A strong proposal should consider questions such as: Who will lead the society after establishment? How will membership be maintained? How will future activities be financed? How will early-career researchers participate? How will leadership transition occur? How will institutions across the region be represented? How will communication between members continue? How will the network measure its development? The stronger the pathway from the initial activity to a functioning organization, the more convincingly the proposal will reflect the purpose of the programme. Diversity and Inclusion Building a neuroscience community also requires thinking carefully about who is included. Although the material supplied does not reproduce every detailed review criterion from the full call, the programme’s broader community-building approach makes representation and participation highly relevant. Applicants should consider diversity across areas such as: Gender Career stage Institution Geography Neuroscience discipline Professional background A national or regional society dominated by one institution may struggle to represent the wider neuroscience community effectively. Applicants can strengthen their proposals by demonstrating meaningful participation from a broad range of researchers. Supporting Early-Career Neuroscientists Emerging societies can play an important role in supporting: Graduate students Postdoctoral researchers Early-career academics Young clinicians New research groups A sustainable scientific society can give these researchers access to: Mentoring Networking Training Collaboration Leadership experience Scientific visibility Applicants may therefore consider how their proposed society or network will create opportunities for emerging researchers. Strengthening Regional Scientific Collaboration The Seeding Neuroscience Grants can also help overcome fragmentation between institutions. In some regions, neuroscientists may work in: Universities Hospitals Medical schools Psychology departments Biomedical laboratories Engineering departments Computational research centres without having a common platform. A formal neuroscience society or network can create stronger links between these communities. This can contribute to: Interdisciplinary collaboration Shared research initiatives Training Resource exchange Regional visibility International partnerships Thematic Networks and Specialized Neuroscience Fields Thematic networks are particularly useful when researchers share a scientific specialization but are geographically dispersed. IBRO explicitly welcomes proposals for new formal thematic networks that do not yet exist as recognized bodies. Examples cited by IBRO include: Computational neuroscience Glial research A successful thematic network could potentially: Connect laboratories Develop shared research priorities Organize specialist training Create mentorship relationships Support collaborative publications Advocate for investment in the field The proposal should still explain how the network will become formal and sustainable. Grant Amount The official programme page identifies the: Maximum grant amount: “See call details.” The public text supplied does not specify a numerical maximum. For accuracy, applicants should therefore consult the current 2026 call documents and IBRO Grants Portal for the applicable funding ceiling rather than relying on older grant figures or unofficial third-party summaries. Open the official IBRO application portal Grant Type IBRO classifies the Seeding Neuroscience Grants under: Event organization However, the purpose is more specific than ordinary event funding. The funded event or organizational activity must contribute directly to establishing a formal neuroscience: Society Sub-society Regional chapter Thematic network Applicants should therefore avoid interpreting the “event organization” classification as general conference support. Application Period The 2026 application period is: 1 September 2026 to 30 September 2026. Applicants should prepare their proposal well before the final day because first-time users will need to create an account on the IBRO Grants Portal. How to Apply Applications must be submitted through the: IBRO Grants Portal Apply for the 2026 Seeding Neuroscience Grants First-time portal users must create an account. Create an IBRO Grants Portal account Applicants experiencing technical difficulties can use the customer support mechanism available through the Grants Portal. IBRO also recommends consulting the portal FAQ where necessary. Before Starting an Application Applicants should first determine whether the proposed initiative truly fits the programme. Consider the following questions: Are we actively trying to establish a formal neuroscience society, sub-society, regional chapter or thematic network? Is our group genuinely representative of an emerging neuroscience community? Is there an unmet scientific or organizational need? Do our planned activities result in concrete governance or institutional outcomes? Will the proposed structure continue after the grant? If another neuroscience society already exists, can we explain why our proposed group adds value? Are we applying for organization-building rather than simply funding a conference? If the answer to these questions is unclear, the project may need further development before submission. What a Strong Proposal Should Demonstrate 1. A Clear Need Explain why the proposed society or network is necessary. Provide context about: Existing neuroscience activity Institutional gaps Geographic fragmentation Lack of formal networking structures Underrepresented neuroscience disciplines 2. A Concrete Establishment Plan Avoid vague ambitions such as: “We hope to create a neuroscience community.” Instead, explain what will actually happen. For example: Convene founding members Draft governance rules Establish an interim executive committee Develop membership procedures Register the organization Adopt a strategic plan Launch formal communication channels 3. Clear Outcomes The project should produce outcomes that can be demonstrated. Possible outcomes could include: Approved constitution Founding committee Membership framework Formal society registration process Strategic plan Regional chapter structure Thematic network governance system 4. Sustainability Explain how the community will continue after IBRO support ends. Potential sustainability mechanisms could include: Membership dues Institutional support Future sponsorship Partnerships Volunteer leadership Future grants 5. Broad Community Engagement Demonstrate that the initiative represents more than a small circle of colleagues where possible. The proposal can be strengthened by engaging researchers from: Different institutions Different cities or regions Different career stages Relevant neuroscience disciplines Applications From Countries With Existing Societies Applicants in countries where a formal national neuroscience society already exists should be especially careful. They should clearly establish that they are pursuing: A formal sub-society A thematic organization A regional chapter and that the proposed body serves a need not currently met by the existing society. The proposal should not appear to create unnecessary duplication. It should instead demonstrate: Complementarity and added value. Application Deadline The deadline is: 30 September 2026 The application period opened on: 1 September 2026 Applications must be completed through the official IBRO Grants Portal. Future Application Rounds IBRO indicates that the next application round is expected to open around the same period next year. Scientists who are not ready to submit in 2026 may therefore consider: Developing their founding group Building institutional partnerships Clarifying the scientific focus Drafting governance structures Joining the IBRO newsletter so that they are better prepared for a future call. Key Details at a Glance Programme: IBRO Seeding Neuroscience Grants Organizer: International Brain Research Organization Purpose: Establishing new neuroscience societies, sub-societies, regional chapters and thematic networks Grant type on IBRO website: Event organization Eligible regions: Africa, Asia-Pacific and Latin America Applications open: 1 September 2026 Deadline: 30 September 2026 Eligible applicants: Groups of scientists and organizations working toward the formation of a formal neuroscience community Examples of supported activities: Governance planning, strategic workshops and other inaugural organizational activities Standalone conferences: Not eligible unless connected to an actionable society/network establishment plan Countries with an existing society: Applicants may seek support for a new formal sub-society, regional chapter or thematic network where clear added value and unmet need can be demonstrated Maximum grant amount: Not numerically stated in the supplied public-page text; applicants should consult the active call details Application method: IBRO Grants Portal Conclusion The IBRO Seeding Neuroscience Grants 2026 provide an important opportunity for scientists in Africa, Asia-Pacific and Latin America to move from informal scientific collaboration toward the establishment of formal, sustainable neuroscience communities. Unlike a conventional conference grant, the programme is specifically designed to support the organizational foundations required to create new: National neuroscience societies Regional neuroscience societies Formal sub-societies Regional chapters Thematic neuroscience networks Funding may support inaugural activities such as governance discussions, strategic workshops and other organizational steps that lead directly to the establishment of a durable scientific body. The programme is particularly relevant in regions where neuroscience researchers currently lack a formal structure for collaboration and professional exchange. It may also support specialized groups in countries where a national neuroscience society already exists, provided the proposed new structure addresses an unmet need and offers clear added value. The most important principle for applicants is that the proposed activity must lead somewhere concrete. A standalone conference or scientific meeting is not enough. Applicants need to demonstrate an actionable pathway toward establishing a society, chapter, sub-society or thematic network. Applications opened on 1 September 2026 and must be submitted through the IBRO Grants Portal by: 30 September 2026. To explore more global grants opportunities, VISIT HERE . title: PhD Scholarship at La Trobe University: Research Opportunity on Family Violence Safety for First Nations and Culturally Diverse Families
summary: La Trobe University is offering a prestigious PhD scholarship opportunity for a doctoral researcher interested in family violence, family court systems, cultural safety, Indigenous and culturally and linguistically diverse families, child and family wellbeing, and long-term safety outcomes. The scholarship forms part of a major Australian Research Council (ARC) Discovery Project examining how safety from domestic and family violence develops and changes for parents involved in family court litigation. The successful PhD candidate will have the opportunity to contribute to an important body of research investigating what helps parents and children move from situations of high risk toward sustained safety, particularly among First Nations and Culturally and Linguistically Diverse (CALD) families . The PhD will be based at La Trobe University and will be supported by experienced researchers from the University s Bouverie Centre, alongside cultural consultants and collaborators connected with the Australian family court system. PhD Scholarship Overview This doctoral opportunity is particularly suited to applicants who are passionate about understanding family violence and improving outcomes for families navigating complex legal, social and service systems. The research will focus on experiences of safety among First Nations and culturally and linguistically diverse parents who have been involved in family court proceedings. Rather than looking only at the presence of family violence or the level of risk experienced by families, the research seeks to understand a broader and equally important question: What helps families become safer after initially being identified as being at high risk? The successful candidate will investigate the personal, family, cultural, community, service and court-related factors that may contribute to improved and sustained safety. This is an opportunity to undertake doctoral research that combines academic research with real-world implications for family courts, family violence services, communities, parents and children. Scholarship Value The scholarship provides: $36,000 per year Funding for 3.5 years Full-time PhD study Research opportunities connected to a major ARC-funded Discovery Project Supervision from experienced researchers in family violence, family court processes and research methodology Opportunities to develop expertise in culturally appropriate research methods Access to the research environment of La Trobe University s Bouverie Centre Opportunities to contribute to research intended to improve safety outcomes for families involved in the family law system The scholarship is funded through La Trobe University s contribution to the ARC Discovery Project. About the ARC Discovery Project The PhD is connected to the Australian Research Council Discovery Project titled: “Enhancing Safety from Family Violence Through and Beyond Family Court Litigation.” The wider project will investigate experiences of safety from domestic and family violence among parents involved in Australia s family court system. The project is designed to follow families over a period of four years after entry into the family court system , allowing researchers to examine what happens not only while families are under the supervision of the court but also after the court s direct involvement decreases or ends. This longer-term approach is important because safety can change over time. A family that is considered high risk when entering court may experience different circumstances several months or years later. The research therefore seeks to understand: How safety changes over time. Which factors are associated with improved safety. Which factors are associated with continued risk. Whether court-based triage processes contribute to improved safety. How family, cultural, personal and social circumstances influence safety. How court management and family circumstances interact. What parents themselves identify as contributing to improved safety. What personal and service-related costs are associated with achieving sustained safety. Focus of the PhD Research The PhD will specifically investigate Research Question 2d of the wider ARC Discovery Project: “To what do First Nations and Culturally and Linguistically Diverse parents attribute improved safety after initial high risk?” The doctoral candidate will have an opportunity to refine the precise research questions in collaboration with the supervisory team. The research may explore several important areas. 1. Factors that support sustained safety The research will examine the factors that help families achieve and maintain safety. These factors could include: Family relationships. Community support. Cultural connections. Access to appropriate services. Personal circumstances. Social support. Interactions with government and statutory systems. Family court processes. Safety planning. Service responses to family violence. Connections to country and community. Experiences of children and parents. Access to culturally appropriate support. The study will consider whether these factors operate differently for First Nations families and culturally and linguistically diverse families. 2. Experiences of mothers following high-risk assessments Another important aspect of the research concerns how First Nations and culturally and linguistically diverse mothers experience safety when they have previously been identified as being at high risk. The research will seek to understand their experiences over time rather than examining safety at only one point. This can provide a deeper understanding of how circumstances change during and after family court proceedings. 3. Parents explanations of improved safety The PhD will also explore how parents themselves explain changes in their circumstances. Instead of relying exclusively on professional assessments or administrative data, the research will provide an opportunity for parents to describe: What changed in their lives. What they believe helped them become safer. Which services were helpful. Which services were difficult or harmful. The role of family and community. The importance of culture. The role of country and connection. Their experiences with the family court. Their interactions with statutory systems. Their experiences after court involvement decreased. What helped them protect themselves and their children. This approach is intended to provide a richer understanding of family safety from the perspective of people who have experienced these circumstances themselves. Expected Research Approaches and Methods The PhD is expected to use several complementary research approaches. The successful candidate will work with the supervisory team to refine the research questions and develop culturally informed methodologies appropriate for the study population. The proposed PhD-by-publication may involve three major approaches. 1. Review of global Family Court practices The first component may involve examining family court practices internationally. The research will investigate practices involving Indigenous and culturally and linguistically diverse populations that seek to improve: Cultural safety. Physical safety. Psychological safety. Family safety. Access to justice. Appropriate engagement with court processes. Support for parents and children. Responsiveness to cultural and community contexts. This component could help identify practices that may contribute to safer experiences for families throughout family court litigation. 2. Analysis of existing research data The second component will involve analysis of data that has already been collected. The available dataset contains information on 214 First Nations and Culturally and Linguistically Diverse parents and their initial safety profiles when they entered the court system. The candidate may compare these initial safety profiles with those of non-Indigenous parents and examine patterns that could contribute to understanding differences in risk and safety. This provides an opportunity for the PhD candidate to develop advanced skills in research data analysis and interpretation. 3. Yarning and narrative approaches The third component is expected to involve a yarning approach with existing cohort participants. Yarning can provide an opportunity for participants to share their experiences through culturally appropriate forms of conversation. In this research, the approach is intended to help participants tell their unfolding stories of safety over time. The research will explore the role of: Community. Country. Family. Service systems. Government and statutory systems. Family courts. Personal experiences. Relationships. Cultural identity and connection. Experiences of risk and safety. Other narrative methods may also be considered. The project specifically notes that approaches such as drawings and artwork are encouraged where appropriate. This creates an opportunity for the research to move beyond conventional interview-based methods and explore ways of allowing participants to communicate experiences of safety in forms that are meaningful to them. Why This PhD Research Is Important Domestic and family violence can have long-lasting effects on parents and children, particularly when families are involved in complex legal proceedings. Family court litigation can itself be a challenging experience, especially for people who are already dealing with violence, trauma, separation, parenting disputes and concerns about the safety of their children. For First Nations and culturally and linguistically diverse families, additional cultural, social and systemic considerations may influence how they experience the court system and services around it. Understanding these experiences is therefore essential for developing approaches that are not only legally appropriate but also culturally responsive and genuinely focused on safety. The research could contribute to improved understanding of: How families move from high-risk circumstances toward greater safety. Why some families experience improved outcomes while others continue to experience risk. How culture influences experiences of safety. How community and family relationships contribute to wellbeing. How service systems can better support families. How family courts can respond more effectively to diverse communities. How culturally appropriate research methods can improve understanding of family violence. How parents and children can be better supported during and after court proceedings. Research Supervisors The PhD candidate will be supervised by a multidisciplinary research team with expertise in family violence, family relationships, research methodology and family court-related research. Primary Supervisor: Dr Anna Booth Dr Anna Booth will serve as the Primary Supervisor for the PhD project. Co-Supervisors The candidate will also be supported by: Dr Felicity Painter Professor Jennifer McIntosh Together, the supervisors will provide expertise in research methodology, analysis and the broader field of family violence and family court research. They will also assist the candidate in developing research outputs and publishing findings from the project. Cultural Support and Research Mentoring An important feature of this PhD opportunity is the emphasis on culturally appropriate research. The candidate will receive cultural support and consultation from Alison Elliott , Bouverie s First Nations team leader. The research team will also encourage links with the Family Courts Indigenous Advisor at the Melbourne Registry . This support is particularly relevant because the project involves research with First Nations families and requires approaches that are respectful, culturally informed and appropriate for the communities involved. The candidate will also be mentored in early-career research through the Bouverie Centre at La Trobe University. They will receive support in developing knowledge of: Domestic and family violence theory. Family court research. Research methodology. Culturally appropriate research. Qualitative research approaches. Quantitative data analysis. Narrative research. Academic writing. Research publication. Working collaboratively with community and professional stakeholders. Who Can Apply? This scholarship is available to domestic applicants only . The opportunity is particularly encouraging applications from: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students who meet the University s PhD candidature requirements. Applicants whose proposed research aligns closely with the project s focus on Indigenous and culturally and linguistically diverse Australian families. The project states that if a suitable First Nations or Culturally and Linguistically Diverse candidate is not available, applications from other students whose research interests align with the project s goals may also be considered. Academic and Research Fit This opportunity may be particularly suitable for applicants with academic or professional interests in areas such as: Nursing and health sciences. Public health. Social work. Psychology. Sociology. Indigenous studies. Family studies. Social policy. Criminology. Law and family law. Child and family wellbeing. Domestic and family violence. Community development. Human services. Gender studies. Mental health and wellbeing. Research methodology. Indigenous health and wellbeing. Culturally responsive practice. Applicants should, however, assess their eligibility against La Trobe University s formal PhD admission requirements rather than relying solely on their disciplinary background. What the Successful PhD Candidate Will Do The successful candidate will become part of a broader research program examining family safety through and beyond family court litigation. Their responsibilities are expected to include: Refining the PhD research questions in collaboration with the supervisors. Developing culturally appropriate research methods. Reviewing relevant international and Australian literature. Examining global family court practices. Analysing existing research data. Investigating safety profiles of First Nations and culturally and linguistically diverse parents. Engaging with existing research participants using appropriate approaches. Conducting qualitative and/or quantitative analyses. Exploring parents experiences and explanations of improved safety. Examining the influence of family, community, culture, country and service systems. Developing research publications. Presenting research findings through appropriate academic and professional channels. Contributing to the wider ARC Discovery Project. Completing a PhD by publication. Skills Applicants Can Develop This PhD can provide valuable research and professional development opportunities. Depending on the final research design, the candidate may develop skills in: Research design. Qualitative research. Quantitative research. Data analysis. Narrative research. Yarning methodologies. Culturally responsive research. Indigenous research approaches. Family violence research. Family court research. Academic writing. Research publication. Critical analysis. Interdisciplinary collaboration. Community-engaged research. Research ethics. Working with sensitive research topics. These skills can be valuable for future careers in academia, research institutions, government, social policy, health, family services, community organisations and other areas concerned with family wellbeing and safety. The Wider Stories of Family Safety Study The PhD is connected to the Stories of Family Safety Study , which forms part of the broader research program. The wider work is interested in understanding safety as something that can change over time. Rather than treating safety as a single outcome measured at one point, researchers seek to understand the journey families experience and the factors that contribute to changes in safety. The research therefore places considerable importance on people s lived experiences and their explanations of what helped them become safer. Background to the Research The project builds on previous research conducted by the team. This includes the ARC Linkage Project: “Family Violence Triage in Family Courts: Safety, Efficacy and Benefit.” That earlier project examined domestic and family violence screening and triage processes within Lighthouse , an innovative approach implemented by the courts to identify family violence risks among litigants. The earlier work focused on improving safety outcomes for families involved in the family law system. The new Discovery Project builds on this foundation by examining safety over a substantially longer period. This creates an opportunity to investigate what happens to families not only during their involvement with the court but also during the period after court oversight and involvement decreases. Application Process Applicants interested in the scholarship should review La Trobe University s formal requirements for applying for a research degree. The application process should be approached carefully because this is a research-based doctoral opportunity rather than a standard taught postgraduate program. Applicants should ensure that they: Meet the University s PhD candidature requirements. Confirm their domestic applicant status. Review the scholarship conditions. Consider how their academic and research background aligns with the project. Prepare the required application materials. Clearly demonstrate their interest in family violence, family safety, culturally responsive research or a closely related area. Explain how their experience and research interests align with the proposed PhD. Review the formal application instructions provided by La Trobe University. Read How to APPLY HERE Scholarship Deadline Deadline: Not specified in the information provided. Prospective applicants should not assume that the absence of a deadline means applications remain open indefinitely. It is advisable to confirm the current closing date directly with La Trobe University or the project supervisor before preparing or submitting an application. How to Get Further Information Applicants who require additional information about the scholarship or research project can contact the primary supervisor: Dr Anna Booth Email: a.booth@latrobe.edu.au Applicants can also visit the official website HERE Key Takeaways This PhD scholarship offers an opportunity to undertake doctoral research within a major ARC-funded research project focused on family violence and safety. The key features include: Degree: PhD University: La Trobe University Research centre: Bouverie Centre Scholarship: $36,000 per year Duration: 3.5 years Study mode: Full time Research focus: Safety from family violence Primary populations: First Nations and Culturally and Linguistically Diverse families Research setting: Family court and post-court contexts Methods: Potentially literature/documentary research, quantitative analysis, yarning and narrative approaches Publication: Expected PhD by publication Supervisors: Dr Anna Booth, Dr Felicity Painter and Professor Jennifer McIntosh Cultural support: Alison Elliott and connections with the Family Courts Indigenous Advisor Eligibility: Domestic applicants only First Nations applicants: Particularly encouraged to apply International applicants: Not eligible based on the information provided Deadline: Not stated; applicants should confirm directly Conclusion The La Trobe University PhD Scholarship attached to the ARC Discovery Project represents a significant opportunity for a researcher interested in family violence, family court systems, Indigenous and culturally diverse families, cultural safety and long-term family wellbeing . By combining existing cohort data with culturally informed research approaches, including yarning and other narrative methods, the PhD candidate will have the opportunity to capture perspectives that may not be visible through conventional court or administrative data. The research could make an important contribution to family violence prevention, family court practice, culturally responsive services and policies designed to improve the safety and wellbeing of parents and children. For eligible domestic applicants with a strong interest in this area, particularly Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander researchers and candidates whose work aligns with the project s focus, this is an opportunity to contribute to research with significant academic, social and practical relevance. title: IAEA Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme 2026/2027: Fully Funded Master’s Scholarship for Women in Nuclear-Related Fields
summary: The IAEA Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme (MSCFP) is an international scholarship initiative designed to encourage and support young women who want to build careers in nuclear science, nuclear technology, nuclear safety, nuclear security, nuclear medicine, nuclear law and other nuclear-related disciplines. Established by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) , the programme provides financial support to selected female students pursuing master s degrees in nuclear-related fields at accredited universities. In addition to financial assistance for master s studies, selected students may also have access to limited internship opportunities facilitated by the IAEA. The programme is particularly valuable for women who want to develop specialist expertise in a field where women remain underrepresented and subsequently contribute to the peaceful, safe and secure applications of nuclear science and technology. The IAEA MSCFP is therefore more than a conventional university scholarship. It is an opportunity to obtain advanced academic training while positioning yourself for a future career in the international nuclear sector. About the IAEA Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme The IAEA Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme was created to inspire more young women to pursue educational and professional opportunities in nuclear-related fields. The programme recognizes the importance of developing a highly skilled workforce capable of contributing to the safe, secure and peaceful use of nuclear science and technology. Through the MSCFP, selected students receive financial assistance toward their master s studies in approved nuclear-related disciplines. The programme may also provide limited internship opportunities facilitated by the IAEA, allowing eligible students to gain exposure to professional environments connected to their academic specialization. The initiative is named after Marie Skłodowska-Curie , one of history s most influential scientists and a pioneer in the study of radioactivity. The programme s broader objective is to encourage the next generation of women scientists, engineers, researchers, legal experts and professionals to enter and contribute to the nuclear field. The IAEA has reported substantial participation in the programme since its launch. Its 2025 reporting stated that 760 students from 129 Member States had been selected since the programme began in 2020, with recipients studying in 76 countries. What Does the IAEA MSCFP Scholarship Cover? One of the major attractions of the IAEA Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme is the level of financial support available to successful applicants. Selected students may receive: Up to €20,000 for tuition costs Up to €20,000 for living costs Potential internship opportunities facilitated by the IAEA Exposure to an international professional and academic network in nuclear-related fields This means that the maximum support described under the programme can reach up to €40,000 , consisting of up to €20,000 toward tuition and up to €20,000 toward living expenses. The actual amount awarded can depend on the applicant s circumstances and the programme s assessment of the financial support required. Applicants who already have another scholarship for their master s programme must declare it to the IAEA. Where additional scholarship funding exists, the IAEA s financial support may be adjusted accordingly. The programme s financial arrangements are therefore designed to prevent undisclosed duplication of scholarship support. Who Can Apply for the IAEA Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellowship? The MSCFP has specific eligibility requirements, and applicants should carefully review them before beginning an application. 1. Applicants must be female The programme is specifically designed to encourage more women to pursue careers in nuclear-related disciplines. Therefore, the programme is open to female candidates who meet the academic and programme requirements. 2. Applicants must be from an IAEA Member State The programme is open to students from IAEA Member States . This means that eligibility is determined by the applicant s country being a Member State of the International Atomic Energy Agency rather than by a particular continent or region. Applicants from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, the Middle East, the Pacific and other regions may therefore be eligible if their country is an IAEA Member State. 3. Applicants must be accepted into or enrolled in a master s programme Applicants must either: Have been accepted into an accredited university master s programme; or Already be enrolled in an accredited university master s programme. The master s programme must be related to an eligible nuclear-related field. An applicant who has not yet secured admission to an eligible master s programme should therefore pay particular attention to the admission requirement before applying. Academic Requirements Academic performance is an important component of the MSCFP selection process. The programme indicates that preference is given to candidates with above-average academic credentials , specifically: 75% or above , or A GPA greater than 3.0 out of 4.0 . Meeting the academic benchmark does not necessarily mean an applicant will automatically receive the fellowship. Selection also considers other factors, including educational background, previous achievements, motivation, career objectives and commitment to public service. Applicants should therefore avoid assuming that academic grades alone determine the outcome. Eligible Fields of Study The IAEA MSCFP supports master s programmes in fields connected to nuclear science, nuclear technology and the wider peaceful applications of nuclear energy. Eligible or relevant fields include areas such as: Nuclear Engineering Nuclear engineering focuses on the design, operation, safety and technological development of nuclear systems and facilities. Students interested in reactor technology, nuclear energy systems and related engineering applications may find this field particularly relevant. Nuclear Physics Nuclear physics examines the properties, structure and interactions of atomic nuclei. It is an important foundation for many applications of nuclear science and technology. Nuclear Chemistry Nuclear chemistry involves the study of radioactive materials, nuclear reactions, radioisotopes and chemical processes associated with nuclear science. Nuclear Medicine Nuclear medicine uses radioactive materials for diagnosis, imaging and treatment of disease. This area is particularly relevant to students interested in the intersection between healthcare and nuclear technology. Isotopic Techniques Isotopic techniques have applications across areas such as medicine, agriculture, environmental science, hydrology, food safety and scientific research. Radiation Biology Radiation biology examines the effects of ionizing radiation on living organisms and biological systems. This field is important in areas including radiation protection, medicine and nuclear research. Nuclear Safety Nuclear safety focuses on preventing accidents and minimizing risks associated with nuclear facilities, materials and technologies. Nuclear Security Nuclear security concerns measures designed to prevent, detect and respond to unauthorized access, theft, misuse or other malicious activities involving nuclear and radioactive materials. Nuclear Non-Proliferation Nuclear non-proliferation deals with efforts to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons while supporting peaceful applications of nuclear technology. Nuclear Law Nuclear law combines legal principles with the regulatory requirements surrounding nuclear activities. It can involve areas such as nuclear safety, nuclear security, liability, safeguards, regulation and international nuclear cooperation. The IAEA provides a broader list of eligible and related fields, meaning applicants should not automatically assume that their programme is ineligible simply because its title does not exactly match one of the examples above. Why the Field of Study Matters Applicants should understand that the MSCFP is not a general master s scholarship. The programme is specifically connected to the IAEA s mandate and therefore focuses on disciplines that can contribute to the safe, secure and peaceful use of nuclear science and technology. For example, a general master s programme that has no meaningful connection to nuclear science, technology, safety, security, medicine, law or another relevant area may not qualify. Applicants should therefore carefully compare their intended programme with the IAEA s list of supported fields before applying. Required Application Documents Applicants are required to submit supporting documents in addition to completing the online MSCFP application form. The required documents include the following: 1. Passport or National ID Applicants must provide a copy of an accepted identification document, such as: Passport; or National identification document. Applicants should ensure that the document submitted is clear and readable. 2. University Admission or Acceptance Letter Applicants must provide an official acceptance or admission letter from the university where they will undertake their master s programme. The document should indicate: The university; The master s programme; The nuclear-related field of study; and The duration of the programme. This is an important document because the IAEA needs to establish that the applicant has been accepted into an appropriate programme. 3. Tuition Fee Statement Applicants must submit documentation showing the tuition costs associated with the master s programme. This may include an official statement or confirmation from the university detailing the applicable tuition fees. 4. Information About Other Scholarships If the applicant has received or is receiving another scholarship for the master s programme, documentation relating to that scholarship must also be submitted. Applicants are required to disclose other scholarship funding because the IAEA may adjust its financial support when another scholarship is available. 5. Reference Form Applicants must arrange for referees to complete the required IAEA reference template. At least one reference is mandatory , while a second reference is preferred . An important point is that the references must be sent directly by the referees to the MSCFP email address by the application deadline. Applicants should therefore contact their potential referees early rather than waiting until the final day of the application period. All Application Documents Must Be in English The IAEA requires application documents to be submitted in English . If an applicant s original documents are written in another language, the applicant must also provide an official English translation. This requirement is particularly important for international applicants because incomplete documentation or missing translations can affect the assessment of the application. The IAEA explicitly states that incomplete applications will not be considered . Applicants should therefore review their application carefully before submission and ensure that every required document has been provided. See Application Form HERE How the IAEA MSCFP Selection Process Works The selection process is competitive. Applications are reviewed by the IAEA MSCFP Technical Selection Committee . The committee assesses applications against several selection criteria rather than considering academic performance alone. The assessment includes: Meeting the programme s entry requirements; Educational background; Previous academic and professional achievements; Motivation for pursuing the programme; The potential impact of the fellowship on the applicant s career goals; Commitment to public service. The IAEA may also consider factors such as: Geographic diversity; Field-of-study diversity; Linguistic diversity; and Other programme-related considerations. This means applicants should prepare an application that tells a clear story about their academic background, professional ambitions and intended contribution to the nuclear field. What Should Applicants Emphasize in Their Applications? Because the selection process goes beyond grades, applicants should make sure their application clearly explains why they want to pursue a nuclear-related career . A strong application should demonstrate a logical connection between: Previous education → chosen master s programme → nuclear-related career goals → potential impact on society → commitment to public service. Applicants should also explain how receiving the fellowship could help them contribute to their country, region or the wider international community. For example, an applicant interested in nuclear medicine could explain how advanced training could contribute to improved access to nuclear diagnostic or therapeutic technologies. Similarly, someone interested in nuclear safety could explain how specialist training could contribute to stronger safety systems, regulation or technical capacity. Internship Opportunities The MSCFP also provides limited internship opportunities facilitated by the IAEA. These opportunities can provide students with exposure to professional environments connected to nuclear science and technology. The IAEA has reported that MSCFP graduates have subsequently been confirmed for internships within IAEA departments and laboratories as well as external organizations, including IAEA Collaborating Centres and other public and private sector partners. Internship opportunities can be particularly valuable because they may allow students to complement academic study with practical professional exposure. However, applicants should understand that the fellowship s primary purpose is master s-level study and that internship opportunities are described as limited . Commitment to Public Service Commitment to public service is one of the factors considered during the selection process. This is significant because the programme is intended not simply to finance individual education but to contribute to the development of a skilled workforce capable of supporting the safe, secure and peaceful use of nuclear science and technology. Applicants should therefore consider how their education and future career can contribute to areas such as: Public health; Nuclear safety; Radiation protection; Energy security; Scientific research; Environmental protection; Nuclear security; Nuclear regulation; Nuclear medicine; Food and agriculture; Water resources; International cooperation; or Other peaceful applications of nuclear technology. Financial Support and Other Scholarships Applicants who already have financial support from another scholarship must disclose that funding to the IAEA. The IAEA explains that its financial support may be reduced where another scholarship exists. In particular, the IAEA may provide only tuition support rather than both tuition and living-cost support for the relevant period. Transparency is therefore essential. Applicants should not omit information about other scholarships in an attempt to receive additional funding. Failure to provide relevant information in a timely and transparent manner may lead to suspension of the IAEA s financial support. Fellowship Acceptance Successful applicants will receive an offer from the IAEA. Selected candidates are required to confirm acceptance of the fellowship within one week . The fellowship offer will contain important information concerning: The value of the award; Payment arrangements; Expected commitments; Administrative requirements; and Other arrangements relating to the fellowship. Successful applicants should therefore carefully read the fellowship offer before accepting it. Obligation to Complete the Master s Programme The MSCFP is intended to support students through their master s education. Selected students are therefore expected to successfully complete the master s programme. Failure to graduate or failure to meet the requirements associated with the scholarship can have serious financial consequences. According to the programme information, failure to meet the scholarship requirements may result in termination of the award and an obligation to repay tuition and living-cost support received from the IAEA upon request. Applicants should therefore apply only when they are prepared to commit themselves fully to completing the master s programme. Who Should Consider Applying? The IAEA MSCFP may be particularly suitable for women who want to pursue advanced education and careers in areas such as: Nuclear engineering; Nuclear physics; Nuclear chemistry; Nuclear medicine; Radiation biology; Nuclear safety; Nuclear security; Nuclear non-proliferation; Nuclear law; Isotopic techniques; and Other fields connected to the peaceful applications of nuclear science and technology. It may also be relevant to students who want to combine nuclear expertise with broader careers in research, healthcare, regulation, international development, public policy or scientific innovation. Why This Fellowship Is a Valuable Opportunity The MSCFP stands out because it combines financial support, advanced academic training and potential professional exposure . For eligible women, the programme can help remove some of the financial barriers associated with pursuing an international or specialized master s degree. The potential benefits include: Financial assistance The programme offers up to €20,000 toward tuition and up to €20,000 toward living expenses, subject to the programme s terms and the applicant s circumstances. Specialized education Students can pursue master s-level education in highly specialized areas connected to nuclear science and technology. International exposure The programme brings together students from IAEA Member States and supports the development of an internationally connected nuclear workforce. Professional development Eligible recipients may have access to internship opportunities facilitated by the IAEA, providing potential practical exposure alongside academic study. Career development Specialized master s-level training can help prepare graduates for careers in scientific research, healthcare, engineering, regulation, nuclear safety, nuclear security, international organizations and other related sectors. Contribution to society The programme is designed around the broader objective of strengthening human capacity for the safe, secure and peaceful use of nuclear science and technology. Read details about this Opportunity HERE Tips for Preparing a Strong Application Applicants should begin preparing well before the deadline. Start with university admission Because an official admission or acceptance letter is required, prospective applicants should identify suitable master s programmes and begin the university application process early. Confirm that your programme is nuclear-related Do not rely solely on the title of your master s programme. Review the programme curriculum and compare it with the IAEA s eligible fields. Prepare your academic documents Make sure your academic records clearly demonstrate your educational background and achievements. Applicants with grades meeting or exceeding the stated academic preference should highlight their academic strengths. Choose referees early Since at least one reference is mandatory and the reference must be sent directly by the referee, applicants should approach referees well in advance. Develop a strong career narrative Clearly explain: Why you want to study the chosen field; Why the field matters to you; How the master s programme fits into your career; How the fellowship will help you achieve your goals; and How you intend to contribute to society after completing your studies. Demonstrate public-service motivation Because commitment to public service is part of the selection criteria, applicants should clearly communicate how their future expertise can benefit their community, country, region or the international community. Check every document Incomplete applications will not be considered. Before submitting, applicants should confirm that they have included all required documents and that documents originally issued in other languages have appropriate English translations. Conclusion The IAEA Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme represents a significant opportunity for women who want to pursue advanced education and build careers in nuclear science, nuclear technology and related disciplines. With financial support of up to €20,000 for tuition and €20,000 for living costs , the programme can substantially reduce the financial burden associated with master s-level study. Beyond financial assistance, the programme can provide a pathway toward professional development and potential internship exposure within the wider international nuclear community. However, this is a specialized fellowship rather than a general master s scholarship. Applicants must be female, come from an IAEA Member State, and be accepted into or enrolled in an accredited master s programme in a nuclear-related field. Strong academic performance is preferred, with the programme indicating 75% or above or a GPA greater than 3.0/4.0 as the preferred academic benchmark. Applicants should also pay close attention to the supporting-document requirements, English-language requirements, reference process, disclosure of other scholarships and the obligation to complete the master s programme. For women interested in nuclear engineering, nuclear physics, nuclear medicine, radiation science, nuclear safety, nuclear security, nuclear law, non-proliferation and other related areas, the MSCFP can provide an important opportunity to gain advanced education and develop expertise that can contribute to the safe, secure and peaceful applications of nuclear science and technology. Because application dates can change from one cycle to another, prospective applicants should always verify the current application deadline and latest eligibility requirements on the official IAEA MSCFP page before submitting an application. title: NASA Lunar Dust Mitigation Intern 2027: Apply for a Hands-On Undergraduate Research Internship at NASA Glenn Research Center
summary: NASA is offering an exciting Lunar Dust Mitigation Intern opportunity for students interested in materials engineering, aerospace engineering, materials science, laboratory research, coatings, vacuum systems, and the technologies needed to support future lunar exploration. Based at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, Ohio, this full-time, in-person internship provides students with the opportunity to contribute to research addressing one of the important technical challenges associated with operating on the Moon: lunar dust. The internship is part of NASA’s Spring 2027 intern session and will involve hands-on laboratory work alongside NASA personnel. Students will assist with the development, characterization, and testing of passive coatings designed to reduce the adhesion of lunar dust to surfaces. The deadline to register is September 14, 2026 . About the NASA Lunar Dust Mitigation Internship Lunar dust presents a significant challenge for future Moon missions. The Moon’s surface is covered by extremely fine particles of lunar regolith, and these particles can be abrasive, electrically charged, and difficult to control. Lunar dust can interfere with mission operations in several ways. It can reduce visibility, change the optical properties of surfaces and equipment, and interfere with mission-critical components. Because future lunar exploration will involve increasingly complex spacecraft, instruments, habitats, vehicles, and other equipment operating on or around the lunar surface, developing effective approaches to managing lunar dust is an important area of research. NASA is therefore investigating passive lunar dust mitigation coatings . These coatings are intended to reduce the amount of lunar dust that adheres to surfaces without requiring external electrical power or continuous human interaction. The selected intern will assist NASA personnel in developing these coatings and evaluating how well they perform under environmental conditions relevant to lunar missions. What the Intern Will Work On The internship is designed to provide substantial hands-on laboratory experience. The intern will work with NASA personnel on research related to the development and testing of materials intended to mitigate lunar dust. Depending on the specific research activities assigned, the work may include: Depositing coatings onto surfaces using sputter deposition . Characterizing the physical and material properties of coating materials. Testing coating performance. title: Julius Baer Graduate Programme 2027: Global Graduate Jobs, Rotations and Career Opportunities in Wealth Management
summary: Are you a recent university graduate looking to build an international career in banking, finance, wealth management, technology, data science, business administration, management, law, risk, or related fields ? The Julius Baer Graduate Programme 2027 offers an opportunity for talented graduates to begin their professional careers with one of the world s established wealth management institutions. Julius Baer is opening recruitment for its 2027 Graduate Programme , providing graduates with structured professional development, practical experience and exposure to different areas of the financial sector. The programme is designed around an 18-month graduate journey featuring three rotations , allowing participants to gain experience across different functions while developing their professional knowledge and skills. Recruitment for the April 2027 cohort opens in September 2026 , while applications for the October 2027 cohort open in February 2027 . This makes the programme particularly relevant for university graduates who are planning their transition from higher education into the financial services industry. Importantly, Julius Baer encourages graduates from a broad range of academic backgrounds to consider the programme. Although specific study profiles are highlighted, candidates whose degrees fall outside the listed fields are also encouraged to apply if they have an interest in the financial sector and specialized knowledge that could contribute to the organization. What Is the Julius Baer Graduate Programme 2027? The Julius Baer Graduate Programme is a structured early-career programme designed to help university graduates develop the knowledge, experience and professional capabilities required to establish a career in wealth management and financial services. Rather than placing graduates into a single function for the entire programme, the graduate journey includes three rotations over 18 months . This rotational structure gives participants the opportunity to gain exposure to different teams and areas of the organization. Through the programme, graduates can explore where their academic background, professional interests and skills are best suited within the broader financial services environment. The programme s overall philosophy is captured by Julius Baer s graduate recruitment message: Be the future. Be Bär. The programme therefore represents an opportunity for young professionals to learn, contribute and develop their careers while gaining exposure to the future of wealth management. Julius Baer Graduate Programme 2027 Key Features The 2027 programme offers several features that make it attractive to graduates seeking structured entry into the financial sector. 1. An 18-Month Graduate Programme Participants undertake an 18-month programme designed to provide a structured transition from university into professional employment. The length of the programme provides graduates with sufficient time to develop practical skills, understand different business functions and build professional relationships. Rather than treating graduate recruitment as a short-term placement, the programme provides an extended development journey. 2. Three Professional Rotations A central feature of the programme is its three rotations . During the 18-month period, graduates have the opportunity to work across different areas of the organization. Rotations can help participants: Develop practical professional experience. Understand how different teams contribute to wealth management. Discover areas that align with their skills and interests. Develop cross-functional knowledge. Build relationships with colleagues across the organization. Gain a broader understanding of financial services. Strengthen their professional profile for future career opportunities. The rotational structure can be particularly valuable for graduates who have strong academic foundations but are still determining which area of financial services they would like to pursue long term. 3. Exposure to the Wealth Management Industry The programme is positioned within the wealth management sector, providing graduates with the opportunity to develop knowledge of an industry that combines finance, investment, advisory services, technology, risk management and client-focused solutions. This exposure can help participants understand how different professional disciplines work together to support financial services organizations. 4. The programme brochure provides further information about these tracks, what the programme offers and the requirements for candidates. This structure allows graduates to learn more about the possible career pathways available to them and identify opportunities that correspond with their academic and professional interests. These include: Accounting, Banking and Finance Graduates with backgrounds in accounting, banking and finance may find opportunities in areas such as: Finance; Advisory; Markets; and Portfolio Management. These areas are particularly relevant for candidates who enjoy working with numbers, financial analysis, markets and investment-related concepts. Graduates interested in financial markets may find the programme useful for developing practical knowledge beyond what is acquired through academic study. Business Administration, Management and Law Candidates with backgrounds in business administration, management or law may explore opportunities connected with areas such as: Transformation; Business Management; Risk; and Legal functions. These disciplines are valuable within financial institutions because successful wealth management organizations require professionals who understand organizational strategy, business operations, regulatory considerations, governance and risk. As financial services become increasingly dependent on technology, data, digital platforms and advanced analytical capabilities, professionals with technical expertise can play an important role in the evolution of wealth management. Graduates From Other Academic Fields Can Also Apply One of the most important aspects of the Julius Baer Graduate Programme is that candidates should not automatically exclude themselves simply because their degree is not one of the study profiles listed by the organization. Julius Baer specifically states that university graduates with degrees in fields not mentioned in the highlighted study profiles should not be allowed to be discouraged from considering the programme. The organization says it is always looking for young talent interested in the financial sector and possessing specialized knowledge in other areas. This means that graduates from nontraditional academic backgrounds may still have an opportunity if they can demonstrate relevant skills, knowledge, motivation and an interest in financial services. Candidates should therefore evaluate their overall profile rather than focusing exclusively on whether the exact name of their degree appears on the list. What Can Graduates Gain From the Programme? The Julius Baer Graduate Programme is designed to provide more than an entry point into employment. Cross-functional exposure Three rotations can provide broader exposure than a conventional entry-level position limited to one department. Career exploration Rotations allow graduates to understand different functions and identify areas where their strengths and interests are best aligned. Professional development An 18-month structured programme provides an extended period in which participants can develop their professional capabilities. Industry knowledge Participants can gain exposure to wealth management and the broader financial services industry. Networking Working across different teams can allow graduates to establish professional relationships with colleagues and other professionals within the organization. Technology and innovation exposure Graduates in data science and information technology can potentially contribute to technology-driven developments within financial services. Opportunities for specialized talent The programme s openness to graduates from academic fields beyond the specifically highlighted disciplines creates room for candidates with specialized knowledge to bring different perspectives to the financial sector. October 2027 cohort Applications for the October 2027 cohort open in February 2027 . Graduates who are not applying for the April intake can therefore consider the later 2027 cohort. Instead of requiring graduates to make a permanent career decision immediately, the programme provides exposure to multiple areas. A participant can use each rotation to develop a better understanding of: The responsibilities of different functions. The skills required in each area. The relationship between departments. Data analytics, digital platforms, information technology, automation and other technological capabilities increasingly influence how financial institutions operate and deliver services. Julius Baer s inclusion of Data Sciences and Information Technology among its study profiles demonstrates the relevance of technical expertise within its graduate recruitment strategy. Graduates with technical backgrounds can therefore consider how their knowledge can be applied to financial services rather than limiting their career search to traditional technology companies. For example, a graduate from a technology discipline could emphasize data and digital skills, while a law graduate could demonstrate knowledge relevant to legal and regulatory environments. The strongest applications are likely to connect the applicant s academic background and skills with the needs of the financial services industry. Connect your degree to financial services Do not simply list your academic qualifications. Explain how your education has developed skills that could be valuable in a financial institution. 4. Highlight transferable skills Graduates should consider emphasizing skills such as: Analytical thinking; Communication; Problem-solving; Teamwork; Leadership; Research; Digital skills; Data analysis; Adaptability; and Ability to learn quickly. 5. Prepare for rotational work Because the programme includes three rotations, applicants should demonstrate that they are comfortable learning new functions, adapting to different teams and working across different areas. 6. Monitor the recruitment windows Candidates interested in the April 2027 cohort should monitor opportunities from September 2026 , while those targeting the October 2027 cohort should begin monitoring openings from February 2027 . 7. The 18-month duration and three-rotation structure make the programme particularly suited to graduates seeking a structured early-career pathway rather than a conventional entry-level position with limited exposure to other areas. Conclusion The Julius Baer Graduate Programme 2027 offers an attractive early-career pathway for university graduates interested in wealth management, banking, finance, technology, data science, business management, law and related fields.
